saints.name: St. Benedict
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The father of Western monasticism, whose Rule of “pray and work” shaped the life of Europe for centuries…
biography: Born about 480 at Nursia in Umbria of a noble family, Benedict was sent to study in Rome but soon fled the city, taking refuge at Enfide and then in a cave at Subiaco, where the monk Romanus clothed him with the monastic habit. There he lived three years as a hermit.

Disciples gathered, and when the monks of a neighboring house, chafing at his strictness, tried to poison him, the cup shattered at his sign of the cross; a raven, Gregory the Great tells us, carried off a second poisoned loaf. At Subiaco he founded twelve monasteries.

About 529 he withdrew to Monte Cassino, destroyed the pagan shrine there, and wrote the Rule that orders the monastic day around the work of God, sacred reading, and labor — ora et labora — tempered with such discretion that it became the pattern of religious life throughout the West. Nearly all we know of him comes from Gregory's Dialogues.

He died about 547, days after his twin sister Scholastica, and was buried beside her at Monte Cassino. Paul VI named him patron of Europe in 1964; he is likewise invoked against poisoning, for the cups that could not harm him.
saints.knownFor: Writing the Rule that founded Western monasticism.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; patron of Europe (1964)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 July
